title: Lagrange Multipliers
body:
Optimising $f$ subject to a constraint $g = k$, without solving the constraint for one variable and
substituting. [[Optimization]] in [[CALCULUS 1]] eliminated the constraint by hand at step 3; that
becomes impossible as soon as $g$ is anything awkward, and this method never needs to.

$$
\nabla f = \lambda \nabla g, \qquad g(x,y) = k
$$

Three equations (two components plus the constraint) in three unknowns ($x$, $y$, $\lambda$).
Solve, then evaluate $f$ at each solution and compare, because the method produces candidates and
does not label them.

## The geometric argument

The whole thing follows from one fact from [[Multivariable Chain Rule]]: **the gradient is
perpendicular to level curves**.

Walk along the constraint curve $g = k$, watching the level curves of $f$ you cross. While you are
crossing them, $f$ is still changing, so you are not at an extremum. At the best point the
constraint curve must be **tangent** to a level curve of $f$: you have stopped crossing them. Two
curves tangent at a point have parallel normals, and the normals are $\nabla f$ and $\nabla g$, so
they are parallel:

$$
\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g
$$

That is the entire derivation, and it is worth reconstructing rather than memorising, because it
also tells you when the method breaks: it needs $\nabla g \neq \mathbf{0}$ at the solution.

```
maximise f = xy  subject to  x + y = 10

∇f = ⟨y, x⟩,  ∇g = ⟨1, 1⟩
y = λ, x = λ    →  x = y
x + y = 10      →  x = y = 5,  f = 25
```

The rectangle of fixed perimeter is a square again, the same answer the substitution method gives,
reached without ever solving for $y$.

## What $\lambda$ means

Not a bookkeeping device. $\lambda$ is the **rate at which the optimal value changes as the
constraint is loosened**:

$$
\frac{d f^*}{dk} = \lambda
$$

Economists call it the shadow price, and it is the reason the multiplier is reported rather than
discarded. Several constraints get several multipliers, $\nabla f = \lambda\nabla g + \mu\nabla h$,
and the geometry is the same: the gradient of the objective lies in the span of the constraint
gradients.

## Where this goes

Constrained optimisation is everywhere downstream. **[[Principal Component Analysis]] is exactly
this problem**: maximise variance $\mathbf{v}^\top C\mathbf{v}$ subject to
$\lVert\mathbf{v}\rVert = 1$, and the Lagrange condition turns into
$C\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$, an [[Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors|eigenvector]] equation with the
multiplier as the eigenvalue. That is why the principal components are eigenvectors and why the
eigenvalue is the variance captured, and it is the cleanest example in the degree of a multiplier
turning out to be the quantity you actually wanted.

Regularisation in [[MACHINE LEARNING]] is the same trade in the other direction: a penalty term
added to a [[Loss Function]] is a constraint on the weights with $\lambda$ chosen instead of solved
for.
